blocks.purpose: Confront the #1 misconception — that passive voice is always an error — by making the learner pick the sentence where passive is the deliberate, correct choice.

options.text: "Passive voice is always bad writing. Every sentence you write in the passive voice is an error you should fix."
options.whyNot: Tempting because teachers flag a lot of lazy passive sentences. But passive voice is a choice, not a crime. Writers use it on purpose when the receiver of the action matters more than the doer, or when the doer is unknown.

options.text: "Twelve laptops were stolen from the lab overnight. Anyone with information is urged to come forward."
options.whyNot: This one survives. The doer is unknown, so active voice would have to invent or dodge a subject. Passive puts the stolen laptops — the thing readers care about — in the spotlight. This is the deliberate, correct use of passive.

options.text: "The essay was being written by me, and then it was being edited by me too, and it was being finished late."
options.whyNot: Tempting because it looks formal and grammatical. But nothing here needs passive: the doer (me) is known and the active verbs 'I wrote, I edited, I finished' would be shorter and stronger. This passive just pads the sentence.

data.prompt: One of these claims is wrong about passive voice. Read all three and pick the one that survives scrutiny.

data.title: Auditor's Eye: Find the Broken Shift

blocks.purpose: Apply voice and mood choices to an unfamiliar real-world writing scenario, justifying each choice for tone and emphasis.

data.decisionPrompt: Write the one-sentence status update the lab will send to the client.
data.decisionPlaceholder: Write one sentence using the voice you chose.

misconception.detail: If you made the intern the subject ('An intern corrected the samples...'), you shifted the client's attention from the passing samples to the mistake itself. When the receiver of the action matters more than the doer — or the doer should stay out of the spotlight — passive voice is the deliberate, correct choice.
misconception.title: Blaming the doer on purpose

data.rationalePrompt: Explain why the voice you chose fits the supervisor's goals for this email.
data.rationalePlaceholder: Name what the voice emphasizes and why that helps here.
data.referenceNote: You may lean on the rule card: active emphasizes the doer; passive emphasizes the receiver; mood sets condition vs fact.

rule.name: Voice matches emphasis
rule.statement: Choose active voice when the doer of the action deserves the spotlight; choose passive voice when the receiver of the action, or the action itself, matters more than who did it.

data.scenarioBody: You intern at a water-quality lab. Overnight, one of your coworkers mixed up two sample labels — an honest mistake. The samples were rerun and everything passed. Your supervisor needs to email the client a one-sentence status update tomorrow morning. The client mainly wants to know: are the results trustworthy? The supervisor also does not want the email to name and shame the intern, though the intern is a known person. Decide which voice the sentence should use, then write the sentence itself.

targetAnswer.decision: Passive voice, for example: "A labeling error was corrected and all samples were rerun; every result now meets the required standards."
targetAnswer.rationale: The rule says to pick the voice that puts the right thing in the spotlight. The client's real question is whether the results are trustworthy, so the samples and the passing results — the receivers of the actions — deserve the emphasis. Passive voice ('was corrected', 'were rerun') keeps the focus on the tests and their outcome while letting a known doer stay out of the spotlight. Active voice would make the intern the subject and turn a reassurance into a blame report.

checks.prompt: A school news post reads: "The championship banner was cut down and taken overnight." Why is the passive voice the deliberate, correct choice here?
checks.answer: It is passive, on purpose: the doer is unknown, so it emphasizes the stolen poster and its fate.
checks.rationale: The doer is unknown, so an active sentence would have to invent a subject like 'someone'; passive lets the stolen banner — the news itself — be the subject.
checks.hint: Is the doer named or known? Who is the sentence really about?
choices: It is passive, on purpose: the doer is unknown, so it emphasizes the stolen poster and its fate.
It is passive by accident: the writer should name the thief in an active sentence.
It is active, and it wrongly emphasizes the doer instead of the poster.
It is conditional mood, because the thief might never be found.
checks.focus: Recognize when passive voice is the deliberate, correct choice

checks.prompt: Complete the subjunctive sentence with one word: "If I ______ the referee, I would stop the game."
checks.rationale: A hypothetical wish about an unreal situation takes the subjunctive 'were' in the if-clause, never 'was'.
checks.hint: A wish about something that is not true never takes 'was' in the if-clause.
checks.focus: Produce correct subjunctive form ('If I were', 'that he be')

checks.prompt: A paragraph uses 'If the gym were replaced, the team would...' and then continues. Which sentence contains an inappropriate voice or mood shift?
checks.answer: "But if the storm was worse, the season would end early."
checks.rationale: The paragraph's hypotheticals use subjunctive 'were'; the sentence 'if the storm was worse' breaks that established pattern with 'was', which is an accidental shift, not an author's choice.
checks.hint: One sentence slides out of the mood the rest of the paragraph is using.
choices: "Last week, two jerseys were stolen from the locker room."
"The coach demanded that every player be on time."
"But if the storm was worse, the season would end early."
"If I were the captain, I would cancel the trip."

checks.prompt: A nurse gave the wrong dosage, but no one was hurt. The hospital's public notice must avoid naming the nurse and must focus on what happened to the patient. Which voice should the notice use? One word.
checks.rationale: Passive voice shifts the spotlight off the doer and onto the receiver of the action, which is exactly the notice's purpose here.
checks.hint: Which voice keeps the receiver — not the guilty doer — in the spotlight?
checks.focus: Choose voice or mood for a stated purpose and justify it

checks.prompt: Choose the correct word: "______ are four fragments and two run-ons on the board."
checks.rationale: The sentence states that run-ons exist at a location, so the place word 'there' is correct; 'their' shows possession and 'they're' means 'they are'.
checks.hint: One word points to a place; one shows possession; one means 'they are'.
